name: Beef organ / liver diet

image.caption: Flower plaque from NH beef brisket and beef organs noodle shop

lead: Followers eat beef liver and other organ meats such as heart and kidney as a concentrated source of nutrients, a trend spread partly by fitness influencers. The payoff people want is better training, energy and general condition, which feed into a fuller, healthier look.

Liver is described as rich in iron, copper, B vitamins and preformed vitamin A, and as very high in vitamin B12, so it fills micronutrient gaps. Food-science studies have looked at adding organs to ground beef patties; no human trials were found testing the practice for appearance.

paras: People eat liver and other organs as meals, mixed into ground beef, or in other everyday recipes, often as part of a meat-heavy fitness diet. Because the effects come from nutrition status, any change in energy or condition builds over weeks of regular eating.

Excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A, affecting bone, liver and the nervous system, and carries birth risks in pregnancy. A single 68 g slice of beef liver can exceed the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A, so portion size matters. Pregnant people and anyone with liver conditions should be cautious.

angle.text: Organ meats like beef liver are eaten as a dense source of iron, B vitamins and other nutrients, with the aim of better training, energy and skin condition. The route runs through filling nutrient gaps rather than a direct visual change. Its appearance use is based on user reports.

lead: Offal, or organ meat, refers to the internal organs of butchered animals such as liver, heart, kidney, tongue and tripe [1]. Attitudes vary: some cultures treat it as taboo and others eat it daily or as a delicacy, and Wikipedia notes that awareness of its nutritional value has grown in places like Ireland, partly through fitness influencers [1].

Animal liver is described as rich in iron, copper, B vitamins and preformed vitamin A, and as very high in vitamin B12 [2]. The same source states that a single 68 g slice of beef liver exceeds the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A [2].
No human studies found test an organ-meat or liver diet for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Beef liver, heart, kidney and other organs
Iron, copper, B vitamins, preformed vitamin A, B12
3,000 micrograms per day of preformed vitamin A

paras: Wikipedia lists raw pork liver as providing about 134 kcal and 21 g of protein per 100 g, with high iron and riboflavin, and notes that liver nutrients vary among species [2]. Liver is the food in which vitamin B12 was linked to its discovery [2].

Hypervitaminosis A is toxicity from too much preformed vitamin A, which can come from liver, supplements and some prescription drugs [3]. Reported effects include headache and raised intracranial pressure, bone pain and fractures, skin and hair changes and liver damage, with children especially sensitive [3]. The US Institute of Medicine sets a tolerable upper level of 3,000 micrograms per day for adults [3]. Wikipedia says that excess vitamin A in pregnancy can harm babies [2], and that possible pregnancy and liver disease are reasons for close monitoring of vitamin A [3].

Historical accounts describe poisoning from polar bear liver, with an estimated acute toxic dose of about 500 g for a human [3]. Some liver from other species carries other risks, such as mercury in ringed seal liver [2].

No studies found testing a beef organ or liver diet for appearance or body composition in people. Related food-science research has examined the quality and consumer acceptability of ground beef patties made with beef heart, kidney or liver, which are laboratory and sensory studies rather than health trials [4][5].
